teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Neither of these things is actually so. Tap the verb after *sī* in each — what do the two have in common?

teach.say: To talk about what is not so, Latin uses **the contrary-to-fact condition (sī + subjunctive: 'if I were …, I would …'; 'if I had …, I would have …')**. Both halves take the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). In ccf-01 the speaker has no money and buys nothing.

check.ask: Both verbs here are subjunctive. Tap the one that belongs to the sī half.

teach.title: Not so now: the imperfect subjunctive in both halves
teach.say: For something untrue *at this moment*, both verbs go into the imperfect subjunctive. Its endings are the infinitive plus **-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt**: *habē-rem, habē-rēs, habē-ret*. It does not mean past time here — stepping back a tense is simply how Latin says 'not really', exactly as English says 'if I *were* rich'.

check.ask: essem — which tense and mood is it?

teach.title: Not so back then: the pluperfect subjunctive in both halves
teach.say: For something that did not happen and is now past changing, both verbs go into the pluperfect subjunctive, built on the perfect infinitive with **-issem, -issēs, -isset**. The *sī* half says what did not happen; the main half says what therefore did not follow.

teach.title: Each half is timed on its own
teach.say: The two halves need not match: each picks its tense by its own time. *Sī tum didicissēs, nunc sapiēns essēs* — the learning did not happen back then (pluperfect), so the wisdom is missing now (imperfect). *Nisi* is just *sī* with the 'not' built in.

check.ask: esset — which tense is it, and so is that half about now or about the past?

teach.title: Telling it from a real condition
teach.say: A *sī* clause that keeps the indicative (the plain statement form) claims nothing about being untrue: *sī adest, gaudeō* — if he is here, I am glad. The subjunctive is the signal that the speaker is saying it is *not* so: *sī adesset* means he is not here.

check.ask: fuissētis — is it indicative or subjunctive?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: To build one, first decide *when* the unreal thing sits. Now? Both halves imperfect subjunctive. Already over? Both halves pluperfect subjunctive. Then put *sī* (or *nisi*) in front of the first half and nothing at all in front of the second: Latin needs no 'then' and no 'would'.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the pluperfect subjunctive of taceō, first person singular — 'if I had kept quiet, father would not have punished me'.

core.text: For the unreal, Latin uses **the contrary-to-fact condition (si + subjunctive: 'if I were …, I would …'; 'if I had …, I would have …')**. Both halves, the *sī* (if) clause and the main one, take the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). Imperfect for an unreal present: *sī thunnus essem, in marī habitārem* — if I were a tuna, I would live in the sea. Pluperfect for an unreal past: *sī aquam bibisset, nōn mortuus esset* — if he had drunk, he would not have died. Latin name: *condiciō irreālis*.
English steps back in time for the unreal — *if I were rich*, *if I had known* — and adds *would*. Latin has no *would*; the subjunctive does that job.
sī / nisi + imperfect … imperfect = unreal now; pluperfect … pluperfect = unreal in the past. The halves may mix.

invented.en: If I had money, I would buy the book.
If you had come, I would have seen you.

core.text: A real future condition keeps the indicative: *sī vēneris, gaudēbō* — if you come: the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense). The subjunctive says it is not so: *sī venīrēs, gaudērem* — if you were coming.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *utinam Rōmae essem* wishes; *sī Rōmae essem, laetus essem* reasons from the wish to its consequence. Both use the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive; *sī* plus a second clause makes it a condition.

The learner's notes (Week 33, 'Contrafactual Subjunctive'): the action is untrue and merely hypothetical; the imperfect makes a hypothetical set in the present, the pluperfect one set in the past, and the same tenses appear in unreal comparisons — *ille vir ululat tamquam lupus esset* (he howls as if he were a wolf), *cecidit tamquam lapide percussus esset* — and after *potius quam* (rather than): *equō vehor potius quam ambulārem* (after a present main verb classical usage would be *sit*, *ambulem*; the notes' examples follow their own past setting). The notes also count the present subjunctive as the future member of the set, the 'future less vivid': *sī nāvis veniat, salvus sim* — if a ship were to come, I would be saved; *loqueris tamquam veniās*.

Ørberg's chapter 33 builds it from the school scene: *sī magistrō pāruissēs, attentē audīvissēs, rēctē scrīpsissēs, ā magistrō laudātus essēs* — if you had obeyed, listened, written correctly, you would have been praised; *etiam sī industrius fuissem, magister mē nōn laudāvisset*. Chapter 34 has Martial's *vellem sī magis esset anus*. Mixed conditions are common: 'if I had learned then (pluperfect), I would now be wise (imperfect)' is *sī tum didicissem, nunc sapiēns essem*. Choose each half's tense by its own time.
Latin has no word for 'would': the subjunctive does that work by itself.
*Sī vēneris, gaudēbō* uses the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense) for a real future.
